Appendix C Optimisation and sampling protocol for ST-MH NQS ensembles

In what follows, we adopt the notation of Appendix B. Namely for a given configuration x∈𝒞x\in\mathcal{C}, the ST-MH NQS ensemble reads

ψk​(x)=exp⁡[χk​fϑ​(x)+ck],\psi_{k}(x)=\exp\left[\chi_{k}f_{\vartheta}(x)+c_{k}\right], (80)

whereby χk∈ℂ1×h,ck∈ℂ\chi_{k}\in\mathbb{C}^{1\times h},c_{k}\in\mathbb{C} and fϑ:𝒞→ℝh×1f_{\vartheta}:\mathcal{C}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{h\times 1}. We further let ℓk​(x):=ln⁡ψk​(x)\ell_{k}(x):=\ln\psi_{k}(x).

C.1 Sampling

For sampling, we use two complementary modes for estimating the energies and overlaps. The first is per-head sampling, where for each head kk, we run an independent Markov chain targeting qk​(x):=pψk​(x)q_{k}(x):=p_{\psi_{k}}(x) and form simple average over i.i.d. or thinned samples xi∼qkx_{i}\sim q_{k}. This maximises effective sample size (ESS) per head, but yields head-specific supports. The second mode is a shared-mixture sampling (self-normalised importance sampling, SNIS) where a single chain targets the uniform (unnormalised) mixture

qmix​(x):=1K​∑m=1K|ψm​(x)|2,q_{\mathrm{mix}}(x):=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{m=1}^{K}|\psi_{m}(x)|^{2}, (81)

and self-normalised importance weights for head kk are

ωk,i∝|ψk​(xi)|2qmix​(xi),∑i=1Sωk,i=1.\omega_{k,i}\propto\frac{|\psi_{k}(x_{i})|^{2}}{q_{\mathrm{mix}}(x_{i})}\quad,\quad\sum_{i=1}^{S}\omega_{k,i}=1. (82)

Note that normalising constants cancel both in acceptance ratios and in the normalised weights, thus no explicit per-head factors NmN_{m} are needed in the mixture. The per-head ESS is then

ESSk=1∑iωk,i2∈[1,S].\mathrm{ESS}_{k}=\frac{1}{\sum_{i}\omega_{k,i}^{2}}\in[1,S]. (83)

This mixture sampling ensures that all heads see the union of supports from all states, especially early in training, which stabilises overlaps and orthogonality pressure.

C.2 Estimators and cost

For head kk, the Rayleigh quotient is estimated via local energies as

E^k={1S​∑i=1SEl​o​c(k)​(xi),xi∼qk(per-head)∑i=1Sωk,i​El​o​c(k)​(xi),xi∼qmix(mixture).\hat{E}_{k}=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{S}\sum_{i=1}^{S}E_{loc}^{(k)}(x_{i})&\,,\,x_{i}\sim q_{k}\,(\text{per-head})\\ \sum_{i=1}^{S}\omega_{k,i}E_{loc}^{(k)}(x_{i})&\,,\,x_{i}\sim q_{\mathrm{mix}}\,(\text{mixture}).\end{cases} (84)

The normalised overlaps use the ratio form shown in Appendix B. With

Lk​l​(x):=ℓl​(x)−ℓk​(x)=ln⁡ψl​(x)ψk​(x),L_{kl}(x):=\ell_{l}(x)-\ell_{k}(x)=\ln\frac{\psi_{l}(x)}{\psi_{k}(x)}, (85)

an estimator of σk​l\sigma_{kl} is

σ^k​l={1S​∑i=1Sexp⁡[Lk​l​(xi)],xi∼qk,∑i=1Sωk,i​exp⁡[Lk​l​(xi)],xi∼qmix.\hat{\sigma}_{kl}=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{S}\sum_{i=1}^{S}\exp\left[L_{kl}(x_{i})\right]&\,,\,x_{i}\sim q_{k},\\ \sum_{i=1}^{S}\omega_{k,i}\exp\left[L_{kl}(x_{i})\right]&\,,\,x_{i}\sim q_{\mathrm{mix}}.\end{cases} (86)

Collecting σ^k​l\hat{\sigma}_{kl} for all pairs forms the empirical overlap matrix σ∈ℂK×K\mathbf{\sigma}\in\mathbb{C}^{K\times K}.

The ratio form in (86) is unbiased for the unnormalised quantity Σk​l/Nk\Sigma_{kl}/N_{k}, not for the normalised overlap σk​l=Σk​l/Nk​Nl\sigma_{kl}=\Sigma_{kl}/\sqrt{N_{k}N_{l}}. In particular,

𝔼qk​[exp⁡[Lk​l​(x)]]=Σk​lNk=σk​l​NlNk,\mathbb{E}_{q_{k}}\left[\exp\left[L_{kl}(x)\right]\right]=\frac{\Sigma_{kl}}{N_{k}}=\sigma_{kl}\sqrt{\frac{N_{l}}{N_{k}}}, (87)

and the mixture variant to approximate the same expectation under qmixq_{\mathrm{mix}} inherits this scaling. This surrogate is therefore asymmetric in (k,l)(k,l) and scale sensitive to the norms NkN_{k} and indeed is a biased estimator of the normalised overlaps. In practice, two design choices made this surrogate behave well in our simulations: (i) we anneal λ\lambda gently such that heads approach the degenerate manifold before strongly imposing orthogonality pressure, and (ii) the per-sample coefficients used in the penalty include a normalisation-correction (see section C.3 below) on the sampling head that discourages trivial rescaling. For all reported results, we validate by recomputing exact, normalised overlaps post-training (via full enumeration for the small systems), which removes any residual ambiguity due to scaling. The post-training results indeed support the results obtained during the training.

We optimise the weighted energy plus an orthogonal penalty cost

C⁡(Θ)=∑k=1Kwk​E^k​(Θ)+λ​𝒫​(σ^​(Θ)),C(\Theta)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_{k}\hat{E}_{k}(\Theta)+\lambda\mathcal{P}(\hat{\sigma}(\Theta)), (88)

where ∑kwk=1\sum_{k}w_{k}=1. In practice, we found the Frobenius penalty

𝒫⁡(σ)=∥σ−𝟏K∥F2=∑k|σk​k−1|2+∑k≠l|σk​l|2.\mathcal{P}(\sigma)=\lVert\sigma-\mathbf{1}_{K}\rVert^{2}_{F}=\sum_{k}|\sigma_{kk}-1|^{2}+\sum_{k\neq l}|\sigma_{kl}|^{2}. (89)

convenient as it treats diagonal corrections and off-diagonals uniformly and mirrors diagnostics used post-optimisation. A linear anneal of the penalty strength λ\lambda from a small value to its final value helps heads approach the degenerate manifold before enforcing strict orthogonality.

Note that in Appendix B, an equivalent off-diagonal penalty 12​∑k≠l|σk​l|2\frac{1}{2}\sum_{k\neq l}|\sigma_{kl}|^{2} is used, and switching between that and equation (89) only modifies small diagonal terms and corresponding gradients in a straightforward manner.

C.3 Gradients

The standard VMC identities from Appendix B yield the standard gradients shown in equations (71) and (72) whereby now, the expectations are taken with respect to qkq_{k} (per-head) or as SNIS reweighted expectations under qmixq_{\mathrm{mix}}.

For the overlap penalty (89), differentiate through the estimator σ^k​l\hat{\sigma}_{kl} in (86). Let

rk​l​(x):=eLk​l​(x)⟹σ^k​l=∑iω~k,i​rk​l​(xi),r_{kl}(x):=e^{L_{kl(x)}}\implies\hat{\sigma}_{kl}=\sum_{i}\tilde{\omega}_{k,i}r_{kl}(x_{i}), (90)

where

ω~k,i={1S,xi∼qk,ωk,i,xi∼qmix.\tilde{\omega}_{k,i}=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{S}&\quad,\quad x_{i}\sim q_{k},\\ \omega_{k,i}&\quad,\quad x_{i}\sim q_{\mathrm{mix}}.\end{cases} (91)

Now define the convenient product

Wk​l,i:=σ^k​l​rk​l​(xi).W_{kl,i}:=\hat{\sigma}_{kl}r_{kl}(x_{i}). (92)

Then the stochastic gradient contributions that match the Appendix B for the surrogate (86) form up-to the ratio-estimator scaling under importance sampling can be expressed via per-sample coefficients and accumulated across samples/heads.

Specifically, because heads share the trunk fϑf_{\vartheta}, one can assemble the full stochastic gradient from a single reverse-mode sweep through the trunk by forming a scalar function whose gradient equals the gradient of the cost. Concretely, let

F⁡(Θ)\displaystyle F(\Theta) =∑k,i[ck,i,re(E)​ℜ⁡[ℓk​(xi)]+ck,i,im(E)​ℑ⁡[ℓk​(xi)]]\displaystyle=\sum_{k,i}\big[c_{k,i,\mathrm{re}}^{(E)}\Re[\ell_{k}(x_{i})]+c_{k,i,\mathrm{im}}^{(E)}\Im[\ell_{k}(x_{i})]\big]
+∑k≠l∑i[ck​l,i,re(𝒫)ℜ[ℓk(xi)]+ck​l,i,im(𝒫)ℑ[ℓk(xi)]],\displaystyle\quad+\sum_{k\neq l}\sum_{i}\big[c_{kl,i,\mathrm{re}}^{(\mathcal{P})}\Re[\ell_{k}(x_{i})]+c_{kl,i,\mathrm{im}}^{(\mathcal{P})}\Im[\ell_{k}(x_{i})]\big], (93)

such that ∇ΘF​(Θ)=∇ΘC​(Θ)\nabla_{\Theta}F(\Theta)=\nabla_{\Theta}C(\Theta). This implies that with the estimator EkE_{k} of the form (84), and weights ω~k,i∈{1/S,ωk,i}\tilde{\omega}_{k,i}\in\{1/S,\omega_{k,i}\}, then

ck,i,re(E)\displaystyle c_{k,i,\mathrm{re}}^{(E)} =2​ℜ⁡[El​o​c(k)​(xi)−E^k]​ω~k,i,\displaystyle=2\Re[E_{loc}^{(k)}(x_{i})-\hat{E}_{k}]\tilde{\omega}_{k,i}, (94)
ck,i,im(E)\displaystyle c_{k,i,\mathrm{im}}^{(E)} =2​ℑ⁡[El​o​c(k)​(xi)−E^k]​ω~k,i.\displaystyle=2\Im[E_{loc}^{(k)}(x_{i})-\hat{E}_{k}]\tilde{\omega}_{k,i}. (95)

For the penalty term, a choice of per-sample coefficients that matches the unbiased gradient of (89) under the estimator (86) is

ck​l,i,re(𝒫)\displaystyle c_{kl,i,\mathrm{re}}^{(\mathcal{P})} =λ​ω~k,i​ℜ⁡[Wk​l,i],\displaystyle=\lambda\tilde{\omega}_{k,i}\Re[W_{kl,i}], (96)
ck​l,i,im(𝒫)\displaystyle c_{kl,i,\mathrm{im}}^{(\mathcal{P})} =−λ​ω~k,i​ℑ⁡[Wk​l,i],\displaystyle=-\lambda\tilde{\omega}_{k,i}\Im[W_{kl,i}], (97)

for head ll and

ck​k,i,re(𝒫)\displaystyle c_{kk,i,\mathrm{re}}^{(\mathcal{P})} =λ​ω~k,i​(2​ℜ⁡[Wk​l,i]−2​|σ^k​l|2),\displaystyle=\lambda\tilde{\omega}_{k,i}(2\Re[W_{kl,i}]-2|\hat{\sigma}_{kl}|^{2}), (98)
ck​k,i,im(𝒫)\displaystyle c_{kk,i,\mathrm{im}}^{(\mathcal{P})} =λ​ω~k,i​ℑ⁡[Wk​l,i],\displaystyle=\lambda\tilde{\omega}_{k,i}\Im[W_{kl,i}], (99)

for head k, for all k≠lk\neq l. The diagonal terms from ∥σ−𝟏K∥F2\lVert\sigma-\mathbf{1}_{K}\rVert^{2}_{F} are handled analogously.

We note that our use of a biased estimator of the normalised overlaps, as shown in (86), dictates a modification of the single-pass function FF. Namely, differentiating the normalisation in σk​l\sigma_{kl}, the Nk\sqrt{N_{k}} factor contributes a constant centring term for head kk which shows up in the per-sampling coefficient as −2​|σ^k​l|2-2|\hat{\sigma}_{kl}|^{2}. This counters the tendency to reduce rk​lr_{kl} by merely inflating NkN_{k}. Empirically, this steers optimisation toward reducing the numerator Σk​l\Sigma_{kl} of the normalised overlap (hence genuine orthogonality), not just reweighing norms. Finally, we note that an unbiased estimator for such normalised overlaps can be in principle constructed, without the general scheme of the training protocol mentioned here being affected.

Given the above, a single call to reverse-mode automatic differentiation accumulates contributions from all heads through the shared trunk. In contrast, an MT-MH ensemble requires KK separate backward passes (one per trunk).

C.4 Orthogonality residuals

One diagnostic we use during and after training is the Frobenius norm of the head-overlap matrix. In what follows, we heuristically quantify an acceptable range for residual fluctuations in the Frobenius norm during training.

During training, two effects dominate residual fluctuations. Namely:

  • •

    Monte Carlo noise: each entry σ^k​l\hat{\sigma}_{kl} is a sample mean (per-head) or a self-normalised weighted mean (mixture). For xi∼qkx_{i}\sim q_{k} and SS effective samples, then

    Var⁡[σ^k​l]≈vk​lS,vk​l=Varqk​[rk​l​(x)].\mathrm{Var}[\hat{\sigma}_{kl}]\approx\frac{v_{kl}}{S}\quad,\quad v_{kl}=\mathrm{Var}_{q_{k}}[r_{kl}(x)]. (100)

    Under the mixture approach with normalised weights, let sk​l2=∑iωk,i​|rk​l​(xi)−σ^k​l|2s_{kl}^{2}=\sum_{i}\omega_{k,i}|r_{kl}(x_{i})-\hat{\sigma}_{kl}|^{2}. A large-sample approximation then gives

    Var⁡[σ^k​l]≈sk​l2ESSk.\mathrm{Var}[\hat{\sigma}_{kl}]\approx\frac{s^{2}_{kl}}{\mathrm{ESS}_{k}}. (101)

    Aggregating entries (treating them as approximately independent at large batch size), the expected squared Frobenius error admits the crude estimate

    𝔼⁡[∥σ−𝟏K∥F2]≈∑ksk​k2ESSk+∑k≠lsk​l2ESSk.\mathbb{E}[\lVert\sigma-\mathbf{1}_{K}\rVert^{2}_{F}]\approx\sum_{k}\frac{s^{2}_{kk}}{\mathrm{ESS}_{k}}+\sum_{k\neq l}\frac{s^{2}_{kl}}{\mathrm{ESS}_{k}}. (102)

    This motivates a simulation-specific tolerance band

    τ:=∑k≠lsk​l2ESSk.\tau:=\sqrt{\sum_{k\neq l}\frac{s^{2}_{kl}}{\mathrm{ESS}_{k}}}. (103)

    That is, one declares orthogonality within Monte Carlo error if ||σ−𝟏K||F2​\lesssim​2​τ\lvert\lvert\sigma-\mathbf{1}_{K}\rvert\rvert^{2}_{F}\lesssim 2\tau.

  • •

    Stochastic-approximation drift: because λ\lambda is annealed and gradients are noisy, the target σ⁡(Θ)\sigma(\Theta) moves over iterations. Brief rebounds of the Frobenius norm were observed in optimisation to commonly coincide with dips in the ESSk\mathrm{ESS}_{k}, head trajectories crossing nodal surfaces, or when a stronger λ\lambda trades a tiny energy gain for a modest overlap increase. These effects are transient and predicted by the ESS-based band in (102) above.
